Theoretically, how big could you make a fidget spinner?

The fidget spinner probably has no structural considerations at this time. It's most likely just sized for ergonomics. You should be able to consider a 1/3 rotationally symmetric section for analysis; basically just one of its arms on the hub. It's also reasonable to model the plastic as weightless with all the loads applied at the weight in the arm and the reaction force at the center bearing.

If you draw a free body diagram of this, you'll get a cantilever beam of length L (x dir), height h (z dir), and width w (y dir) that has two loads applied at the mass in the arm. One load will be a bending load in -z direction​ due to the gravity acting on the weight. We'll call this F_grav. The other load will be due to the centrifugal force acting on the weight, will be directed in the +x direction, and we can call it F_spin.

To estimate failure, you'll need to look at the internal stresses caused by these two loads. The failure should occur at the bearing where the bending stress is maximum. The pulling stress from the centrifugal force will be uniform throughout the spinner and increase with higher rotational velocities. You'll need to pick a reference speed and combine these stresses together.

You'll find that the mass of the weight and therefore F_grav increases with the cube of the scaling factor. Furthermore, the bending moment increases even faster (by the scaling factor to the fourth power) because it's the product of F_grav and the length of the beam L (which is also growing with the scale). However, the bending stress won't grow so quickly because it is proportional to the bending moment divided by the section modulus. I believe the section modulus is proportional to the square of the beam's height times the beam's width. This would mean modulus grows with the cube of the scaling factor (assuming height and width scale the same). Therefore when you divide the bending moment by the section modulus in order to see how the bending stress depends on scale, we get something to the fourth power divided by something to the third power. This means the bending stress Increases linearly with scaling factor.

F_spin is proportional to the mass of the weight and the distance L from the center of rotation for a given angular velocity. Therefore this force is proportional to the scaling factor to the fourth, just as bending moment in the previous paragraph. The tensile stress here though it's merely force divided by cross sectional area. The cross sectional area is proportional to the square of the scaling factor. Therefore the tensile stress from spinning will be proportional to the square of the scaling factor.

The bending stress will put the top of the beam (+z side) in tension and the bottom (-z side) in compression. The spinning stress will be pure tension. Therefore the failure point to consider will be the top of the beam (where both act in tension and consequently sum) at the bearing (where bending stress it maximum). You'll compare these stresses to the yield strength of your plastic (which won't change with scale). Essentially you'll end up with this equation:

S_yield = stress_bending + stress_spinning

I'll leaves plugging in actual numbers as an exercise for the reader, but as bending stress increases linearly with scale and spinning stress increases quadratically with scale we can say that it doesn't scale perfectly and would eventually break if made too large, particularly if spinning very fast. If you decide to do any calculations, remember to check your units,I'd use SI units, and use radians per second for the angular velocity.

Keep in mind that this neglects the dynamic force of flicking the spinner to get it moving by considering the static case in a rotating reference frame. You could add another bending force in the y-direction to achieve a desired angular acceleration if you want that extra detail.

Let me know if you have any questions.
